claims.text: The Mg-Zn-Cu eutectic additive has a melting range of approximately 340-380 °C.
Adding 2-5 wt% Mg-Zn-Cu powder and sintering at 850 °C produces a transient liquid phase at grain boundaries.
The transient liquid phase accelerates diffusion and improves grain-boundary wetting.
Liquid-assisted particle rearrangement and solution-precipitation promote pore elimination.
The transient liquid suppresses nucleation of coarse, segregated intermetallic phases.
The transient liquid lowers the activation energy for mass transport.
Liquid-phase-assisted mass transport enables substantial densification at 850 °C before significant Mg vaporization occurs.
Mg vaporization typically accelerates above 900 °C.
The liquid phase dissolves segregated transition-metal clusters.
Dissolved transition metals reprecipitate as fine, uniformly distributed precipitates.
The resulting single-phase-like matrix forms a continuous protective oxide scale during subsequent exposure.
Sintering with the additive at 850 °C will produce a relative density greater than 98%.
The resulting microstructure will lack large segregated intermetallic regions.
Oxidation mass gain will be reduced by more than 40% relative to standard-sintered samples.
Mg loss during the proposed process will remain below 1 wt%.
Standard solid-state sintering of the same powder at 900 °C without additives typically produces approximately 92% relative density.
Standard solid-state sintering at 900 °C causes significant Mg volatilization.
Standard solid-state sintering at 900 °C produces a microstructure dominated by coarse, segregated intermetallic phases.
Below 820 °C, insufficient liquid mobility causes porosity greater than 5%.
Above 950 °C, or when no liquid phase is present, Mg loss exceeds 3 wt% because densification relies on high-temperature solid-state diffusion.
